entity.name: Alexander Pushkin
entity.description: The poet who invented modern Russian literature. Pushkin published his first poem at 15, was exiled by two emperors for political verse, and wrote Russia's greatest novel in verse while under surveillance. Part African through his great-grandfather, a kidnapped prince raised by Peter the Great. Killed at 37 in a duel over his wife's honor.

story.name: Alexander Pushkin
story.description: Exile for radical poetry, a verse-novel written under imperial surveillance, marriage to Moscow's most beautiful woman, and a fatal duel at the Black River. The life of Russia's founding literary voice.

moments.name: Alexander Pushkin Is Born into Russian Nobility in Moscow
moments.subtitle: The future father of Russian literature descends from an African prince and ancient boyars
moments.description: On June 6, 1799, Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin was born in Moscow to a noble family with extraordinary ancestry. His father descended from 12th-century Russian nobility. His maternal great-grandfather, Abram Gannibal, was an African boy kidnapped by Ottoman slave traders, gifted to Peter the Great, and raised as the emperor's godson before becoming a general and governor. Pushkin spoke mostly French until age ten, learning Russian from household serfs and his beloved nanny Arina Rodionovna. He would grow up to forge those two linguistic worlds into the foundation of modern Russian literature.

moments.name: A 15-Year-Old Pushkin Publishes His First Poem at the Imperial Lyceum
moments.subtitle: The school's first graduating class produces Russia's greatest poet
moments.description: Around 1814, Alexander Pushkin published his first poem at age 15 while attending the prestigious Imperial Lyceum in Tsarskoye Selo near Saint Petersburg. By graduation, his talent was already widely recognized across Russia's literary scene. At the Lyceum, Pushkin studied under David de Boudry, the brother of French revolutionary Jean-Paul Marat, and absorbed Enlightenment ideas that would soon put him at odds with the Russian state. Upon graduating, he recited his controversial "Ode to Liberty," one of several poems that would eventually lead Emperor Alexander I to exile him from the capital.
moments.address: Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum, Pushkin, Saint Petersburg

moments.name: Pushkin Writes Boris Godunov and Eugene Onegin While Exiled to His Mother's Estate
moments.subtitle: Imperial censors ban the poet from publishing, so he writes his two greatest works
moments.description: From 1824 to 1826, Alexander Pushkin lived in exile at his mother's rural estate of Mikhailovskoye near Pskov, banished by the government for clashing with authorities in Odessa. Under strict surveillance and unable to publish, Pushkin produced his most enduring works: the historical drama Boris Godunov in 1825 and major portions of his verse-novel Eugene Onegin, serialized from 1825 to 1832. Boris Godunov would not receive publication permission for five years, and its uncensored version was not staged until 2007. The forced isolation became the most productive period of Russia's greatest writer's life.

moments.name: Pushkin Marries Natalia Goncharova in Moscow's Great Ascension Church
moments.subtitle: Russia's greatest poet weds Moscow's most talked-about beauty after a year-long delay
moments.description: On February 18, 1831, Alexander Pushkin married Natalia Goncharova at the Great Ascension Church on Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street in Moscow. Goncharova, then 18, was considered one of Moscow's most beautiful women. Their engagement in 1830 had required assurances from the Tsarist government that it would not persecute the libertarian poet, and a cholera outbreak delayed the wedding by a full year. The couple became regulars at court society, but Pushkin's intense jealousy and Goncharova's flirtatiousness set the stage for the fatal confrontation that would end his life just six years later.

moments.name: Pushkin Is Fatally Shot in a Duel at the Black River over His Wife's Honor
moments.subtitle: Russia's greatest poet dies at 37 defending his wife against her sister's husband
moments.description: On January 27, 1837, Alexander Pushkin faced Georges d'Anthes, a French officer who had married Pushkin's sister-in-law yet continued pursuing Pushkin's wife Natalia, in a pistol duel at the Black River near Saint Petersburg. The duel followed months of scandalous rumors and a deliberately insulting letter Pushkin had sent to provoke the challenge. In the "barrier duel" format, both men walked toward each other and could fire at will. D'Anthes fired first, striking Pushkin in the abdomen. Pushkin died two days later on February 10, 1837, at age 37. Russia lost the poet widely regarded as the founder of its modern literature.
